name: Nora Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at Scholaris, which makes software schools use for timetables and messages to parents. Most of my week is fixing small things in the parent app, like a message that went to the wrong class or a timetable that shows two teachers in one room. I use an AI assistant now and then, mostly when I'm stuck and too embarrassed to ask again. I like that the work helps schools, because my mum was a dinner lady for twenty years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a small flat ten minutes from my parents. They run a bakery on Station Road, and on Sundays I help Dad with the accounts and the website. Scholaris was bought last year by a bigger education software group, and there's a lot of talk about teams being merged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a relief to picture, I'll be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that people got carried away with. At work I'd say the real issue is the merger, not AI. I don't post much online, apart from photos of Dad's bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit worried, because the merger rumours were there before any AI talk. If they merge the parent-app teams, the bigger company has its own developers, and I'm the junior. AI not changing much doesn't help me with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to make myself useful in the merger, maybe by writing the guide to how our parent app works. I'd keep my savings at about three months and stop buying lunch out, maybe 60 a month saved. I'd keep using the AI assistant when I'm stuck, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a low hum, not an alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Scholaris would decide if you stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Helen (my team lead), who likes me but isn't the one holding the money. The new group has a manager in another city who's never met me. That's the part I don't like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did lose the job, what would your family do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would tell me to move back home, and Dad would offer me shifts at the bakery straight away. I wouldn't want to, but I know they'd never let me go without. That's what family is for.

say: AI was a **useful tool** that people got carried away with.
The real issue at work is the **merger**, not AI.
think: The **merger rumours** were there before any AI talk.
If teams merge, the bigger company keeps **its own developers** and I'm junior.
do: Write the **guide** to how the parent app works for the merger.
Stop buying lunch out to save about **60 a month**.
Use the AI assistant **when stuck**, as now.
feel: **Uneasy**, a **low hum** rather than an alarm.
S0.quote: Mum would tell me to move back home, and Dad would offer me shifts at the bakery straight away.
fieldNote: Her worry stems from a **merger**, not from AI.
Her **family bakery** is a safety net she'd rather not use.
She'd stay useful by **documenting** the parent app.

steps.text: Write the guide to Scholaris's parent app
Stop buying lunch out to save about 60 monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coding and answering customers. Schools ring us all day, so that's both of my team's jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the way business goes, and firms will use what saves money. I'd say young people should get proper on-the-job training, not just be told to retrain. At work I'd keep my head down and do good work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the merger plus AI means fewer developers and fewer support staff. The new group would use AI to answer schools and fix simple bugs, and I'm on simple bugs. I'd give myself a year, maybe two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI assistant every day once I saw the seniors doing it, so I'm not the one who looks slow. I'd ask Helen if I could move closer to the schools, maybe training teachers on the app, which needs a person in the room. I'd also start building the bakery's online ordering properly on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd keep it to myself. I don't like making a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why training teachers? Couldn't AI do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day. But a teacher who's had a long day wants a person to sit with them, not another screen. I'd bet on that for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build for the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Online orders for cakes and bread for collection, with Saturday slots. Dad loses orders because people ring when he's got flour on his hands. If it works, it could bring in maybe another 300 a month for them.

say: Firms will use **what saves money**; that's business.
Young people need **on-the-job training**, not just a retraining slogan.
think: The **merger plus AI** means fewer developers and support staff.
I'm on **simple bugs**, so I'd give myself a year or two.
do: Use the AI assistant **daily** once seniors do.
Ask Helen to move into **training teachers** on the app.
Build the bakery's **online ordering** on Sundays.
S1.quote: A teacher who's had a long day wants a person to sit with them, not another screen.
fieldNote: She steers toward **people-facing** training, betting on human contact.
Her **traditional** view sees family business as part of her future.
She hides worry because she **doesn't like** making a fuss.

steps.text: Use the AI assistant daily like the seniors
Ask Helen to move into training teachers on the app
Build online cake and bread orders for the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Oh. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together, because the government can't fix this by handing out money. I'd say it at church and at the bakery counter. At work I'd say very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out of software by 2028, and most of my team too. All my work is on a screen. The bakery is hands-on, so Dad's ovens and shaping dough would have until about 2031, but the ordering and accounts I do would go to AI straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd give notice on my flat and move back in with my parents, which saves about 750 a month. I'd work at the bakery on Saturdays and help Dad open a second counter at the market, because people still buy from people. I'd keep my savings untouched as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd failed, even though it wouldn't be my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel you'd failed. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my parents were so proud when I got a job in software. Dad told every customer for a month. Moving home at 27 would feel like going backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what happens to the bakery when robots arrive around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. A robot that shapes bread might be very expensive at first, and a small family bakery might be the last to get one. I'd hope regulars like knowing whose hands made their loaf.

say: **Families and communities** must pull together; handouts won't fix this.
I'd say it at **church** and at the bakery counter.
think: I'm **out of software** by 2028, with most of my team.
The bakery's **hands-on** work lasts until about 2031; its paperwork doesn't.
do: Give notice on the flat and **move home**, saving about 750 a month.
Work **Saturdays** and open a market counter with Dad.
Keep savings **untouched** as long as possible.
feel: **Alarmed**, and feeling she'd **failed** though it isn't her fault.
S2.quote: My parents were so proud when I got a job in software. Dad told every customer for a month.
fieldNote: She splits the **bakery** into hands-on work that lasts and paperwork that doesn't.
**Moving home** is her first and largest money move.
Her alarm carries **shame** about letting her parents down.

steps.text: Give notice on the flat and move back home
Lean on her parents for housing and work
Open a market counter with Dad's bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. Still not long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people to prepare if they're sensible and don't wait for handouts. I'd encourage friends to learn a practical skill. At work I'd say we should be told honestly what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect to lose my developer job before 2031. But five years means I could do the teacher-training role for a while and save properly. And I could help Dad grow the bakery before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the teacher-training role in year one and use AI tools when the others do. I'd build the bakery's online orders and market counter over the first two years, so it can support more than my parents. I'd stay in my flat for now and save 200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a direction. It's like walking in fog with a torch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the bakery really support you as well as your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as it is. With a market counter, online orders and maybe wedding cakes, it might. Mum makes beautiful cakes and nobody knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousins who are choosing courses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Samira, who's sixteen, to learn something with her hands as well as her head. Maybe baking, maybe nursing. And not to borrow a fortune for a degree that a machine can do.

say: There's time to prepare if people are **sensible** and don't wait for handouts.
We should be **told honestly** what the company's plan is.
think: I'd still lose my **developer job** before 2031.
Five years lets me **grow the bakery** before I need it.
do: Ask for the **teacher-training** role in year one.
Grow bakery **orders and market counter** over two years.
Stay in the flat and save **200 a month**.
feel: **Anxious** but with direction, like walking in **fog** with a torch.
S3.quote: I'd tell my cousin Samira, who's sixteen, to learn something with her hands as well as her head.
fieldNote: She turns the **family bakery** into a deliberate long-term plan.
Advice to **cousin Samira** shows her trust in practical skills.
Five years lets her keep her **independence** a bit longer.

steps.text: Ask Helen for the teacher-training role in year one
Grow bakery online orders and a market counter
Save 200 a month while staying in the flat
Use AI tools once the team does

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. That's nearly my whole career so far, times three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should use it to build something solid. I'd say it to the girls at church who are just starting work. At Scholaris I'd say we'd have time to adapt together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I can get properly good at software first. I'd probably make mid-level by 2029. I'd also think about marriage and a family, because that feels possible again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Scholaris and use the AI tools as they become normal. I'd keep helping at the bakery on Sundays and grow the cake orders slowly. Around 2032 I'd decide whether to join the bakery properly, before the robots in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The merger still worries me more than AGI in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said marriage feels possible again. Has it felt impossible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not impossible, but in the fast pictures it feels selfish to plan a wedding. With ten years, I'd let Mum introduce me to people again. She'd be delighted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you join the bakery full time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it made enough to pay two salaries, or if Dad's back got worse. My dad is 58 and lifts flour sacks every morning. The decision to join the bakery might be made for me.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so people should build something solid.
At Scholaris we'd have time to **adapt together**.
think: Ten years lets me get **properly good** at software first.
**Marriage and family** feel possible again with this much time.
do: Keep going at Scholaris and use AI tools **as they become normal**.
Grow the bakery's **cake orders** slowly on Sundays.
Decide around **2032** whether to join the bakery.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the **merger** worrying her more than AGI.
S4.quote: My dad is 58 and lifts flour sacks every morning. The decision to join the bakery might be made for me.
fieldNote: Long warning revives **marriage plans** she sets aside in faster pictures.
Her **father's health** may decide her path more than AI.
The **merger** remains her main short-term worry.

steps.text: Keep fixing the Scholaris parent app
Grow the bakery's cake orders on Sundays
Let Mum introduce her to people with marriage in mind

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be moving home and starting over before I'd had a chance to build anything. What would help is support for small family businesses to grow, like cheap loans, so the bakery could carry more of us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the older generation sees it. Dad thinks software was the safe choice and baking was the risky one. Dad might turn out to have had the safer job all along.

headlineQuote: Dad thinks software was the safe choice and baking was the risky one.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old** junior developer on the parent app at Scholaris, a school software firm.
A **merger** with a bigger group worries her more than AI in milder pictures.
Her **traditional views** lead her to family, church and the bakery rather than the state.
Her parents' **bakery on Station Road** is both her safety net and her plan.
She uses AI **now and then** and adopts it once the seniors do.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, forcing her to move home before building anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** and support so small family businesses can grow.
